conversation.text: Both are optional but frequently expected together on realistic exam scenarios.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: ServiceRequest.specimen references what should be, or was, collected for the request — the same Specimen resource used elsewhere in diagnostics.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: occurrence[x] is when the requested service should happen — a dateTime, a Period, or a Timing, depending on how precise the schedule is.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: That's different from authoredOn, which just marks when the request itself was written.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So specimen answers what to collect, occurrence answers when it should happen — two separate questions on one resource.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Specimen.collection captures how and when it was gathered — method, bodySite, and who did the collecting.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: processing logs anything done to the specimen afterward, like centrifuging or adding a preservative, each with its own time.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: container describes the physical vessel — type, capacity, and any additive already in it.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Together those three elements trace a specimen's whole journey from collection to whatever's tested.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: ImagingStudy is structured in three layers — the study itself, one or more series within it, and individual instances within each series.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: series carries its own modality, like CT or MR, since a single study can mix modalities across different series.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Each instance represents one actual image or object, identified within its series.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So a question about how many images is really asking about instances nested under series, nested under the study.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: ImagingStudy is built to line up with DICOM — series.uid maps to the DICOM Series Instance UID, and instance.uid maps to the SOP Instance UID.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: endpoint on the study or series tells a system where to actually retrieve the images, often via WADO-RS.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: That alignment is deliberate, so FHIR can reference imaging without having to redefine what DICOM already standardized.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Exam tip: if a question mentions UIDs or retrieving actual pixel data, it's pointing you toward ImagingStudy's DICOM alignment, not a generic attachment.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: When you write a MedicationRequest, the drug itself can show up two ways — a plain CodeableConcept code, or a reference to a separate Medication resource.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: You reach for the reference when you need more than a code can capture — batch, lot, manufacturer, or a compounded formulation.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Most simple orders just use medicationCodeableConcept with an RxNorm code — lighter weight, one round trip.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: MedicationDispense and MedicationAdministration follow the same pattern, so check which one a scenario actually needs before assuming a full Medication resource is required.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The Medication resource covers what a code alone can't — form, like tablet or oral solution, plus the full ingredient list.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Each ingredient has an item — a substance code or reference — and a strength expressed as a ratio, like 500 milligrams per tablet.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: There's batch information too: lot number and expiration date, which matters for dispensing safety and recalls.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So if a question asks about composition or strength rather than dosing instructions, you're looking at Medication, not MedicationRequest.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: MedicationRequest has two fields that trip people up — status and intent — and they answer different questions.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Status is where the order stands right now: active, on-hold, completed, stopped, cancelled.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Intent is what kind of request it even is — proposal, plan, original-order, or a filler-order coming from the pharmacy system.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Mixing them up is a classic trap — a 'draft' status doesn't tell you it's just a proposal, that's intent's job.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: dosageInstruction is the sig — how the patient should actually take it: route, timing, dose and rate.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: dispenseRequest is separate — that's what the pharmacy fills: quantity, expected supply duration, and how many repeats are allowed.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So one resource carries both the clinical instructions and the fulfillment logistics, just in different elements.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: If a question is about refills or days' supply, go straight to dispenseRequest, not dosageInstruction.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: MedicationRequest.substitution says whether the pharmacist can swap in a generic — allowed can be a boolean or a coded reason.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That's different from reasonCode or reasonReference, which explain why the medication was prescribed in the first place.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So substitution governs what happens at the pharmacy counter, not why the doctor ordered the drug.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Exam questions like to swap those two — read carefully whether it's asking about substituting the drug or justifying the order.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: MedicationDispense.quantity is what actually left the pharmacy — the real dispensed amount, not what was ordered.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: daysSupply is how long that quantity should last the patient, which payers care about for refill timing.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: There's also whenPrepared and whenHandedOver — two separate timestamps for filling versus actually handing it over.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: If a scenario mentions early-refill flags or supply gaps, daysSupply is the field doing that math.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: MedicationDispense.performer records who did the work — but it's not just one undifferentiated role.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: The function element distinguishes them — data enterer, packager, checker, final checker — each a different step in the dispensing workflow.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So performer isn't just 'the pharmacist' — it's a structured list of everyone who touched that dispense event.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Watch for questions asking which performer function applies to a given verification step — that's testing the code list, not the concept.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: authorizingPrescription links a dispense event back to the order that actually justified it.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It's a reference to one or more MedicationRequest resources, since a single dispense can fulfill several linked orders, like a multi-ingredient compound.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Without that link, you'd have a dispense floating with no traceable authorization — exactly what auditors, and this exam, both check for.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So if a question asks how you prove a dispense was actually prescribed, authorizingPrescription is the answer.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: MedicationAdministration documents an actual event — a clinician gave this dose, at this time, and that's recorded as fact.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: MedicationStatement is softer — it's a record that the patient is, or was, taking something, often self-reported or pulled from history.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: That difference in provenance matters — administration implies clinical accountability, statement doesn't necessarily.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Don't treat a MedicationStatement as proof of administration, and don't chart a reported home medication as MedicationAdministration — that mix-up is a real exam trap.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Across this whole family — Request, Dispense, Administration, Statement — the trick is picking the resource that matches the workflow state described.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: An order that hasn't been filled yet is a Request. Something handed to the patient is a Dispense. A witnessed dose is Administration.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: And anything based on what the patient tells you, rather than what your system documented, is a Statement.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Read the scenario for who's asserting what happened — that's the fastest way to land on the right resource under time pressure.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Immunization.vaccineCode carries the actual vaccine identity — CVX codes are the standard in US contexts.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: lotNumber and expirationDate track the specific product given, which matters enormously for recalls and adverse-event follow-up.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: And status isn't just completed — it also covers not-done, with a statusReason explaining why the dose wasn't given.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So a refused or contraindicated dose is still documented — just with status not-done rather than being left out entirely.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: protocolApplied is how Immunization tracks where a dose fits in a series — dose two of three, say.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It names the series, the authority defining it, like ACIP, and the target disease, plus doseNumber and seriesDoses.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: That's what lets a system say 'this patient is up to date' rather than just listing shots with no context.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: If a question is about tracking series completion or catch-up schedules, protocolApplied is the element in play.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Immunization.reaction captures an adverse event after a dose — a date, a reference to the observed reaction, and whether it was reported by the patient or observed clinically.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: programEligibility is a different concept entirely — a coded element for things like VFC eligibility, whether this dose was given under a publicly funded program.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Pair that with fundingSource, and you can see who's actually paying for the vaccine, separate from the clinical reaction record.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Don't confuse reaction with statusReason — reaction is what happened after the shot, statusReason is why a dose wasn't given at all.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Coverage.subscriber is the policyholder — the person whose name the plan is actually under.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: beneficiary is the patient being covered, which might be the same person or a dependent — a spouse or child, say.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: relationship codes that connection — self, spouse, child — so you know how the beneficiary relates to the subscriber.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Don't assume subscriber and beneficiary are always the same person — that's exactly the distinction the exam tests.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Coverage.payor points to who's actually financially responsible — usually an Organization, the insurance company itself.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: class is where the plan details live — group, plan, subplan — each entry typed with a code plus a value and a display name.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So payor answers 'who pays,' and class answers 'under which specific plan or group.'

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Claims and eligibility checks both lean on class values to route the request to the right benefit package.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Coverage.period sets the effective dates — when this coverage actually applies.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: order is the coordination-of-benefits field — an integer ranking which coverage is primary, which is secondary, when a patient has more than one plan.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Get that wrong and a claim gets sent to the wrong payer first — a very real-world error this element exists to prevent.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So when a scenario mentions multiple insurances, order is the field that decides who pays first.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: CoverageEligibilityRequest is how a provider asks a payer, up front, whether a patient's coverage is active and what it covers.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: purpose narrows the ask — auth-requirements, benefits, discovery, or validation — so the payer knows exactly what kind of answer to send back.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: It's a real-time check, not a claim — nothing's being billed yet, you're just confirming coverage before the visit.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That upfront check is exactly what prevents a denied claim after the fact — it's the whole point of doing it first.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The request references the Coverage through an insurance backbone element, with a focal flag marking which coverage the question is actually about.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Then item describes what's being asked — a category or a specific productOrService, like 'is physical therapy covered under this plan.'

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So you're not asking 'is this patient covered' generically — you're asking about specific services or benefit categories.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That specificity is what lets the payer's response come back itemized instead of a blanket yes or no.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: CoverageEligibilityResponse mirrors the request's items, but now with real numbers — benefit.allowed and benefit.used for each category.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: excluded flags anything not covered outright, and authorizationRequired tells the provider whether they need prior auth before proceeding.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: outcome at the top level — complete, error, or partial — tells you whether you can trust the detail or need to retry.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So this is where the abstract eligibility question turns into an actual answer the front desk can act on.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Claim.type sets the whole context — institutional, professional, oral, pharmacy, vision — because adjudication rules differ by claim type.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: item is the line-by-line detail: sequence, productOrService, quantity, unitPrice, and net — basically an itemized bill.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Get the type wrong and the payer may reject the claim outright before it even looks at the items.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So type answers 'what kind of claim is this,' and item answers 'what exactly is being billed.'

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Claim.diagnosis and Claim.procedure carry the coded reasons behind the claim, each entry sequenced so line items can point back to them.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: diagnosis holds the ICD-10 codes justifying medical necessity, procedure holds what was actually done — CPT or similar.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: supportingInfo is the catch-all for anything else adjudication needs — attachments, prior treatment dates, even lab results — each tagged with a category.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Items reference back to diagnosis and procedure sequence numbers, so the whole claim stays linked instead of being a flat list of codes.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Claim.insurance is a list, not a single coverage, because a patient can have more than one policy in play.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: sequence orders them for coordination of benefits, and focal marks which one this particular claim is actually being submitted to.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: businessArrangement and preAuthRef ride along too, tying the claim to any prior authorization already obtained.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So when a claim bounces between primary and secondary payers, sequence and focal are what track which coverage is being billed at each step.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: ClaimResponse.item.adjudication is where the payer's decision actually lives — category codes like eligible, copay, deductible, benefit, each with an amount.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: And when something's wrong with a specific line, error points right at it — itemSequence, detailSequence, and a code explaining the problem.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So adjudication tells you what was decided, and error tells you what couldn't be processed at all.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Reading those together is how you diagnose a partially-paid or rejected claim instead of just seeing a generic denial.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: ClaimResponse is the payer's formal, system-to-system answer to a Claim — built for the provider's billing system to consume.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: ExplanationOfBenefit carries a lot of the same adjudication data, but it's built for a broader audience — including the patient, through things like CARIN Blue Button data sharing.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: In practice EOB tends to be the richer, more complete record, combining claim and response detail into one resource.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So a payer showing a member their coverage history is EOB territory, not a raw ClaimResponse.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: EOB.benefitBalance tracks running totals against a plan — categories like deductible or out-of-pocket max, each with allowed and used amounts.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: total is simpler — category-tagged summary amounts for the claim itself, like submitted versus paid.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So benefitBalance is about the patient's overall plan standing, while total is about this one claim's bottom line.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: 'How much deductible is left' points to benefitBalance; 'what did this claim actually pay' points to total.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: ExplanationOfBenefit carries the same provider, diagnosis, and procedure detail as the original Claim — provider and careTeam say who was involved.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: diagnosis and procedure mirror the claim's coding, so the payer's response stays traceable back to what was actually billed.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: item is where it gets richer than a plain ClaimResponse — each line item carries its own adjudication detail, not just a top-level decision.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So EOB is really the claim's full story plus the payer's line-by-line judgment on every service rendered.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Account tracks a billing relationship over time — status, the subject it covers, who owns it, and who's guaranteeing payment.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: ChargeItem is the individual billable event — a specific service or supply, with its own code, quantity, and price, linked back to an account.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So Account is the ledger, and ChargeItem is each entry posted to it.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That separation matters when a scenario asks about a running balance versus a single billable event.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Invoice formalizes what's actually owed — status, who it's addressed to as recipient, and a date.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: lineItem references the ChargeItems or describes them directly, each with its own priceComponent — base price, discounts, taxes, surcharges.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: totalNet and totalGross roll all of that up, before and after those adjustments.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So where ChargeItem records that something happened, Invoice is the actual bill assembled from those charges.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: PaymentNotice is a lightweight heads-up — a payer or provider signaling that a payment was made, tied back to the original request.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: PaymentReconciliation is heavier — paymentAmount, paymentDate, and a detail array reconciling each individual claim or request the payment covers.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So notice says 'a payment happened,' and reconciliation says exactly which claims that payment settles and for how much.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: processNote on reconciliation is where explanatory text about the payment run gets attached — useful when one lump payment covers many claims at once.

145.topicTitle: HTTP methods, headers, URLs, and status codes

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: FHIR rides directly on HTTP verbs — GET for read and search, POST for create, PUT for update, DELETE for delete.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: The response status codes carry real meaning too — 201 for created, 200 for a successful read, 404 for not found, 410 if it's been deleted.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Headers matter just as much — Content-Type and Accept tell the server and client what format they're speaking.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Match the verb and the URL shape to the interaction you actually want — that's the whole game on questions about this.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The standard media type is application/fhir+json, or application/fhir+xml if you're working in XML.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Accept tells the server what format you want back, Content-Type tells it what format you're sending — they can differ on the same request.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: There's also a _format query parameter as a fallback, for clients that can't easily set custom headers.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Servers only have to support one format to be conformant, so don't assume both JSON and XML are always available.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Every resource version gets an ETag — a weak validator wrapping the versionId, like W slash quote 3 quote.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: If-Match uses that ETag for a conditional update, so you only overwrite the version you actually read — that's optimistic locking.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: GET and PUT are idempotent — repeat them and you get the same end state — but POST isn't, since it creates a new resource each time.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Miss an If-Match check and you can silently overwrite someone else's concurrent edit — that's the concurrency trap this is testing.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Conditional processing lets a client say 'do this only if' instead of just blindly creating or overwriting.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Conditional create checks If-None-Exist against a search first, so a retried request doesn't leave you with duplicate resources.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Conditional update pairs a search with a PUT, letting the server create or update based on business identifiers instead of a server-assigned id.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It's really about safety over an unreliable network — retries and race conditions shouldn't produce duplicate or corrupted data.

149.topicTitle: Read, vread, create, update, patch, and delete

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: read is a plain GET on type slash id; vread adds _history slash the version id to pull a specific historical version.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: create is POST to the type endpoint, update is PUT to a specific id — and update can create a resource too, if that id doesn't exist yet.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: patch is the odd one out — it takes a JSON Patch, XML Patch, or FHIRPath Patch body to change just part of a resource.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: And delete removes the current version but keeps history — a vread against an old version still works after a delete.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Search uses typed parameters — string, token, date, reference — and each type supports its own modifiers and prefixes.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: _include and _revinclude pull in related resources, and _sort, _count, _summary, _elements shape what comes back and how much.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: history is separate — GET .../_history returns every version of a resource as a Bundle, not just the current one.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Just because a search parameter is in the registry doesn't mean a given server actually implements it — check the CapabilityStatement first.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: CapabilityStatement is a server's self-description — which resources, interactions, search parameters, and operations it actually supports.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Before you assume a server can do chained search or a particular operation, that's the resource to check first.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Operations extend beyond plain CRUD — anything invoked with a dollar sign, like $everything or $validate, is a named operation rather than a standard interaction.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So capabilities tell you what's possible on this server, and operations are the custom verbs layered on top of the standard ones.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Conditional create sends If-None-Exist with a search query — if a match already exists, the server just returns it instead of creating a duplicate.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Conditional update swaps the id in the URL for search parameters, letting the server resolve which resource, or create one if none matches.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Conditional delete works the same way, but if the search matches more than one resource, the server has to reject it rather than guess — that's a 412.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So all three trade a server-assigned id for a search-based match, which is exactly what makes them safe to retry.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Each search parameter has a declared type — string, token, reference, date, number, quantity, uri, or composite — and that type drives how matching works.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: token is exact-match on a code plus optional system, string does partial left-anchored matching by default, and reference lets you search by what a resource points to.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Get the type wrong in your head and you'll misread how a modifier or prefix is supposed to behave on it.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So before reasoning about a search query, identify the parameter's type first — everything else follows from that.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Modifiers attach with a colon — exact, contains, missing, not — and which ones are legal depends on the parameter's type.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Prefixes are different — they go on the value itself for date, number, and quantity searches: gt, lt, ge, le, sa, eb, ap.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So family colon exact equals Smith uses a modifier, while date equals gt 2024 uses a prefix — don't mix up the two syntaxes.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Exam questions love testing whether a modifier is even valid for a given type — string doesn't support the same modifiers token does.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Chaining lets you search on a property of a referenced resource — Observation?subject:Patient.name=Smith finds observations by the patient's name.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Reverse chaining goes the other direction with _has — it finds patients who have a matching observation pointing at them.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So chaining follows a reference forward, and _has follows it backward, from the resource being referenced to the ones referencing it.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Both come with a performance cost, since the server has to resolve through another resource type — worth knowing when scenarios ask about efficient search design.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: _include pulls in resources your matches reference — like including the Practitioner when you search Observations.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: _revinclude goes backward — it pulls in resources that reference your matches, say, the Observations that point at a Patient you searched for.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: _sort and _count control ordering and page size, while _summary and _elements trim the payload down to just what you actually need.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Combine them carelessly, though, and a big _count with unrestricted _include can quietly return far more data than you meant to ask for.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Search results paginate through Bundle.link entries — next, previous, self — so you follow those URLs rather than constructing your own.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: When a query has too many parameters to fit comfortably in a URL, you can POST to type slash _search instead, with the parameters in the body.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The search behaves identically either way — POST-based search isn't a different kind of search, just a different transport for the same query.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That's handy for scenarios with long lists of codes or identifiers that would otherwise blow past URL length limits.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Standard interactions are the fixed, generic verbs every resource type shares — read, search, create, update, delete.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Operations are named, custom behaviors that don't fit that generic CRUD shape — $everything, $validate, $expand — invoked with a dollar sign.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: If what you need is 'get everything related to this patient in one call,' no standard interaction does that — that's exactly why $everything exists as an operation.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So the test is: does this fit the generic verb set, or does it need custom logic? That's what pushes you toward an operation.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Operations are scoped at three levels — instance, type, and system — and the level changes what context they run against.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: An instance-level call like Patient slash 123 slash $everything operates on one specific patient. A type-level call like ValueSet slash $expand runs against the whole resource type.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: System-level operations sit at the root of the server, like $meta-data, with no particular resource type in scope at all.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So before invoking an operation, check its scope — calling a type-level operation at the instance level, or vice versa, just won't resolve.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: $validate checks a resource instance against a profile before you commit to storing it — catching structural or terminology problems early.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: $everything, on a Patient, pulls the whole compartment — encounters, conditions, meds, everything referencing that patient — in one call.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: $expand, $lookup, and $translate are the terminology trio — expand a ValueSet into actual codes, look up details on one code, or translate a code through a ConceptMap.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: And $meta lets you add, remove, or list metadata like tags and profiles, while $document assembles a Composition and its referenced resources into a proper document Bundle.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Parameters exists for operations that need multiple named inputs or outputs that don't naturally fit a normal resource body.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Each parameter entry has a name and a value — value of type x, a nested resource, or even nested parts for structured input.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: $validate is a good example — it needs both the resource to check and, optionally, a profile URL, so those travel together inside a Parameters resource.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So whenever an operation's input or output looks like more than 'here's one resource,' expect Parameters wrapping it.

162.topicTitle: searchset, history, batch, transaction, document, message, and collection

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Bundle.type tells you what kind of bundle you're looking at, and each value means something specific.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: searchset is what a search returns — matched resources plus paging links. history is every version of a resource over time.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: batch and transaction both bundle multiple requests together, but transaction is atomic — all or nothing — while batch processes each entry independently.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: document is a signed, attested snapshot built around a Composition; message pairs a MessageHeader with its payload for event-driven exchange; and collection is just a plain grouping with no special processing implied.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Both batch and transaction package multiple entries into one Bundle, each with its own request — method and url.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: The difference is atomicity: transaction succeeds or fails as a whole, batch just processes each entry independently and reports results per entry.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So if your scenario needs 'all of these updates happen together or none do,' that's transaction, not batch.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Sending a batch when you actually needed atomic behavior is exactly the exam trap here — partial failure is possible and won't be flagged as an error.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Every entry in a Bundle carries a fullUrl — for resources that don't have a server id yet, that's often a urn:uuid placeholder.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That placeholder lets one entry reference another within the same transaction, and the server resolves it to a real reference once everything's created.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: entry.request carries the method and url — what HTTP call this entry represents, like POST Patient or PUT Observation/123.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: And entry.response, on the way back, carries the actual outcome — status code, location, and etag for what was just done.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: In a transaction Bundle, either every entry succeeds or the whole thing rolls back — that's what atomic actually buys you.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That atomicity is what makes provisional fullUrl references safe — you can create a Patient and an Observation that references it in the same transaction, using a temporary uuid.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The server processes the bundle, assigns real ids, and rewrites those internal references before anything is considered committed.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Try that same trick in a batch, and you risk the Observation referencing a Patient that never actually got created — no atomicity to protect you.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: A document Bundle wraps a Composition plus everything it references — it's a signed, point-in-time snapshot, like a discharge summary.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Messaging is different — a MessageHeader plus its payload gets pushed to a receiving system as an event, like 'a patient was just admitted.'

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Documents are about a durable, attestable record; messaging is about triggering something to happen on the other end.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So a discharge packet handed off between systems is a document, while an admission notification is messaging.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Subscription lets a client register criteria — a resource type plus search parameters — and get notified whenever a matching resource changes.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: The channel defines how that notification arrives — rest-hook posts to a callback URL, websocket pushes over an open connection, or it can just be email or a plain message.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: This flips the model from polling — instead of repeatedly asking 'anything new,' the server tells you the moment it happens.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So if a scenario needs near-real-time awareness of new lab results without constant polling, Subscription is the mechanism, not repeated search.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The Bulk Data Access API is built for pulling large populations of data, not one patient at a time — think a whole group or an entire system export.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: You kick it off with a GET to $export — at the system, Group, or Patient level — plus a Prefer: respond-async header, since this isn't a quick synchronous call.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The server responds 202 Accepted with a Content-Location, and you poll that URL until the job finishes.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Once it's done, you get back links to NDJSON files — one resource per line — exactly the shape you want for streaming a huge export instead of one giant JSON blob.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Not everything in FHIR is a quick request-response — bulk export, and some long-running operations, use Prefer: respond-async instead.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: The server immediately returns 202 with a status URL, the client polls it, and eventually gets a completion response instead of waiting on an open connection.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Messaging and Subscriptions push further into event-driven territory — the receiving system reacts when something happens, rather than asking on a schedule.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So the choice isn't just REST versus not-REST — it's picking sync, async-polling, or event-push based on how long the work takes and how fresh you need the data.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: A StructureDefinition is how FHIR formally describes a profile — it constrains a base resource like Patient or Observation into something IG-specific.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It ships two views: the differential, which only lists what you changed from the base, and the snapshot, the fully resolved element list you actually validate against.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Slicing lets you split a repeating element like Observation.component into named, individually-constrained pieces, and FHIRPath invariants add rules that go beyond plain cardinality.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So when an exam question mentions an IG, don't just answer with base R4 cardinality — the profile's constraints are what actually apply.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: A CapabilityStatement is a server's resume — it declares which resources, interactions, search parameters, and operations that specific FHIR endpoint actually supports.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: An ImplementationGuide is different — it's the packaging resource that bundles a whole set of profiles, extensions, and rules into one versioned, publishable deliverable.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So CapabilityStatement answers 'what can this server do right now,' while ImplementationGuide answers 'what does this whole spec require across every server that implements it.'

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Don't confuse the two on the exam — one's runtime discovery, the other's a design-time publication artifact.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: A SearchParameter resource is the formal definition behind every query parameter — it names the parameter, gives its type, and states the FHIRPath expression that extracts the value.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: OperationDefinition does the same job for custom operations — it specifies the dollar-sign name, the parameters in and out, and whether it runs at instance, type, or system level.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Both get advertised in the CapabilityStatement, but just because a SearchParameter is registered doesn't mean a given server actually implements it.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Right — always check what the server's CapabilityStatement actually declares, not just what's in the registry.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: CompartmentDefinition groups resources around an anchor like Patient or Practitioner, so a server can answer 'give me everything in this patient's compartment' in one search.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: GraphDefinition is different — it describes a graph of resource references to follow, which is what powers the $graph operation for pulling a connected set of resources in one call.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Both are conformance artifacts alongside StructureDefinition and CapabilityStatement — they describe structure and behavior, not clinical data itself.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Compartment is about scoping access and search by patient; graph is about traversal. Easy to mix up if you don't anchor on what each one actually returns.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Every profile starts from a base resource — Patient, Observation, whatever — and only ever narrows it. It can't add elements the base doesn't already allow for.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So a profile can tighten cardinality, bind a tighter value set, or fix a value, but it can't loosen a 1..1 into a 0..* or contradict the base spec.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: That's why you validate against the profile, not just the base — the profile is what's actually being asked for in a given IG.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Exam tip built right in: when a scenario names an IG, the profile's constraints win over generic base-resource cardinality.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The differential in a StructureDefinition only lists the elements you actually changed from the base — it's compact, but you can't validate against it alone.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: The snapshot is the fully expanded view — every element from the base plus your constraints, merged into one complete list.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Tooling generates the snapshot from the differential, so authors write the small diff and validators consume the full picture.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: If you're ever reading a profile to understand total structure rather than just what changed, you want the snapshot, not the differential.

176.topicTitle: Cardinality restrictions, fixed values, and patterns

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: A profile can restrict cardinality — narrow a 0..* down to 0..1, or make an optional element required — but it can never widen what the base allows.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: fixedValue is the strict one: the element has to match that exact value, nothing else. patternValue is looser — it just has to include everything specified, extra fields are fine.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So a fixed CodeableConcept means only that one coding is allowed, but a pattern CodeableConcept just means that coding has to be present among possibly others.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That distinction shows up constantly on the exam — 'must equal exactly' is fixed, 'must contain at least' is pattern.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Slicing splits a repeating element into named slices so a profile can put different rules on each one — like requiring specific LOINC codes on different Observation.component slices.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Must Support is separate though — it's the IG telling implementers 'if this element is populated, you have to handle it,' not that it's required to be present.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Right, don't equate Must Support with 1..1 — an element can be optional cardinality-wise and still be Must Support. Is Modifier is the other flag to watch, since it changes how the whole resource is interpreted.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: And binding strength constrains which codes are valid in a coded element — slicing, Must Support, and binding are three separate levers profiles pull, not one thing.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Cardinality and value sets can't express everything a profile needs, so FHIRPath invariants add custom rules — like 'if this component exists, that one has to also.'

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Each invariant has a key, an expression written in FHIRPath, and a severity — error blocks validation, warning just flags it.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: They live right on the ElementDefinition in the StructureDefinition, so a validator evaluates them alongside cardinality and binding checks.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: When a question describes cross-field logic an IG enforces, that's an invariant doing the work, not base cardinality.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: CapabilityStatement.format is where a server declares which serializations it'll actually return — typically application/fhir+json, sometimes fhir+xml, rarely turtle.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: There's also patchFormat for PATCH requests, since JSON Patch, XML Patch, and FHIRPath Patch all have different media types.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: A client should check this before assuming a server speaks XML, since plenty of R4 servers only support JSON now.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So identify the purpose — format negotiation — then map it to the right CapabilityStatement element rather than guessing from the base spec.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: CapabilityStatement.rest.resource lists every resource type a server supports, and for each one it names exactly which interactions — read, search, create, update — are turned on.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It also lists the searchParam entries the server actually implements for that resource, with type and documentation.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So a parameter existing in the FHIR registry doesn't mean this particular server honors it — the CapabilityStatement is the real source of truth.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Same goes for _include, _revinclude, and result-shaping params like _sort, _count, and _elements — check support before you build a query around them.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Beyond basic REST, CapabilityStatement.rest.operation lists which named $operations a server exposes on that resource type — say, $everything on Patient or $validate anywhere.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: And rest.security is where a server declares its auth model — usually a SMART on FHIR extension pointing at the authorize and token endpoints.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So if you need to know whether a server supports a custom operation, or how to authenticate against it, the CapabilityStatement is where you look, not the base spec.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Exam-wise: operations always start with a dollar sign, and security here is about discovery — the server still checks scopes at request time.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: FHIR isn't only REST — Documents bundle a fixed, attested snapshot of resources, like a discharge summary that shouldn't change after it's signed.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Messaging pushes an event-driven payload to a receiver, structured as a Bundle with a MessageHeader describing what happened and who should act on it.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Subscriptions flip that around — a client registers interest and gets notified when matching resources change, and bulk export handles pulling huge extracts asynchronously.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Pick the paradigm by workflow: an interactive app is REST, a discharge packet is a document, and a multi-year population extract is bulk.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Picking the right IG comes down to matching the workflow — US Core is the general floor for domestic clinical data aligned to USCDI.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Da Vinci covers payer-provider exchange — things like prior auth and risk adjustment — while CARIN Blue Button is specifically about giving members access to their own claims.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Bulk Data handles large population-level exports rather than one-record-at-a-time access.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: And always pin both the FHIR version and the exact IG package version — profiles change between IG releases even on the same FHIR version.

184.topicTitle: Profiles, extensions, operations, searches, and examples

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: An Implementation Guide isn't just documentation — as a package it actually bundles StructureDefinitions for its profiles, plus any custom extensions it defines.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It also ships OperationDefinitions and SearchParameters the profiles depend on, so a server implementing the IG knows exactly what custom behavior to support.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: And every serious IG includes example resources — actual instances that validate against the profiles, so implementers have something concrete to test against.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So when you install an IG package, you're pulling in all five of those pieces together, not just a set of constraints on paper.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: IGs are distributed as versioned FHIR packages, similar in spirit to npm packages, each identified by a canonical name and version.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: A package can declare dependencies on other packages — say, a state-specific IG depending on US Core — and those get pulled in and validated together.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Get the dependency versions wrong and your profiles might validate against the wrong base definitions entirely.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So always pin the FHIR version plus every IG package version explicitly — 'latest' is exactly what breaks reproducible validation.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Every profile, ValueSet, or CapabilityStatement has a canonical URL — a globally unique identifier that, combined with a version, pins exactly which definition you mean.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Publishers manage a lifecycle too — draft, active, retired — so consumers know whether a canonical resource is stable enough to build against.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Conformance expectations layer on top: SHALL versus SHOULD language, Must Support flags, all governed by whoever owns that canonical URL.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So when an IG applies, you're trusting its governance and its specific profile constraints — not just generic base cardinality.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: US Core is the baseline IG for US clinical data — it profiles resources like Patient, Observation, and Condition to align with USCDI, the government's minimum data set.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It's the floor almost every other US IG builds on — Da Vinci and CARIN both assume US Core underneath them.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: It defines Must Support elements and required terminology bindings, like requiring specific vital-sign LOINC codes on Observation.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So when a question is about domestic clinical interoperability generally, US Core is usually the default answer.

188.topicTitle: SMART App Launch and Backend Services

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: SMART App Launch handles interactive apps — a clinician launches an app from inside the EHR, and OAuth's authorization code flow hands it a token plus launch context like which patient's chart is open.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Backend Services is for system-to-system access with no user present — that's client credentials, authenticated with a JWT signed by the client's private key instead of a shared secret.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Either way, scopes limit exactly what the token can touch, and your app has to handle 401s and refresh tokens gracefully.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: If a scenario says a patient is chart-browsing, that's SMART plus REST. A nightly batch job with no user is backend services — don't mix those up.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: CARIN Blue Button is built around ExplanationOfBenefit — it's how health plans expose a member's own claims history through a FHIR API.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It sits on top of US Core and adds payer-specific profiles for coverage, patient, and the EOB itself, covering professional, institutional, and pharmacy claims.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The whole point is patient access to their own claims data, which is why it's tied closely to the CMS interoperability rules.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So a member wanting to see their claims history in an app — that's CARIN, not Da Vinci, which is the payer-to-provider side.

190.topicTitle: Da Vinci PDex, Prior Authorization, CRD, DTR, Risk Adjustment, and Clinical Data Exchange

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Da Vinci is a whole family of IGs solving payer-provider workflows — PDex is the core one, letting a payer expose a member's clinical history back to providers or apps.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: CRD and DTR work together for prior auth — Coverage Requirements Discovery uses CDS Hooks to tell a clinician in-workflow whether something needs prior authorization, and DTR then serves up the questionnaire to gather the documentation.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Prior Authorization Support, PAS, is what actually submits that request as a FHIR Claim and gets a real-time decision back, instead of a fax.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Risk Adjustment and Clinical Data Exchange round it out — CDex pulls supporting clinical data for a request, and risk adjustment IGs standardize sharing the diagnosis data payers need for risk scoring.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Bulk Data Access is the $export operation — instead of paging through search results one patient at a time, you kick off an async job at the system, group, or patient level.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: You call $export with a Prefer: respond-async header, the server responds 202 Accepted with a Content-Location URL, and you poll that until the job's done.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Once it's ready, you get back a manifest listing NDJSON files — newline-delimited JSON, one resource per line — that you download and stream-process.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That NDJSON format plus the async kickoff-and-poll pattern is the whole point — it's built for millions of records, not a handful.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: A Coding is one system's way of representing a concept — it needs both system and code to mean anything; display alone isn't enough.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: CodeableConcept wraps one or more Codings plus free text, which is handy when you want to carry both a SNOMED code and, say, a legacy local code for the same concept.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Binding strength tells you how tightly a value set applies — required, extensible, preferred, or example — and that's separate from whether the element itself is mandatory.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Miss the system on a Coding, or use the wrong binding strength, and that's a classic failure mode — the code becomes ambiguous without knowing which code system it came from.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Coding.system is the URI identifying which code system you're using — SNOMED CT, LOINC, whatever — and without it the code by itself is meaningless.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: version is optional, but it matters when a code system's meaning has actually changed release to release, like some LOINC codes over time.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: display is just a human-readable label for the code — it's not authoritative, so don't validate against it, only against system plus code.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: userSelected is the one people forget — it flags which Coding a human actually picked when a CodeableConcept carries more than one, which matters for knowing intent versus a system-added code.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: A CodeSystem is where the actual codes live — it defines the concepts, their meanings, and often a hierarchy, like SNOMED CT's is-a relationships.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: content mode tells you how complete the resource is — complete means every code is listed, fragment means it's a partial example, and not-present means you query it externally.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Concepts can carry properties too — things like status or a parent code — which is what powers operations like $lookup and $subsumes.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Don't confuse CodeSystem with ValueSet — CodeSystem defines what codes exist; ValueSet picks which ones you're allowed to use here.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: A ValueSet is a curated subset of codes pulled from one or more CodeSystems — its compose element lists what to include or exclude, sometimes with filters like 'descendants of this SNOMED concept.'

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: $expand turns that intensional definition into an explicit list of codes a UI or validator can actually use.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: It's the ValueSet that gets referenced in an element's binding, not the CodeSystem directly — the CodeSystem is just where those codes originate.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So think of CodeSystem as the dictionary and ValueSet as the specific word list you're allowed to pick from for this element.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: ConceptMap maps codes from a source system or value set to a target — say, translating a local lab code into the equivalent LOINC code.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: $translate is the operation that actually runs the mapping and hands back the translated coding.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Each mapping carries an equivalence — equivalent, wider, narrower, inexact, or unmatched — so you know how faithful the translation actually is, not just that one exists.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That equivalence matters clinically — treating a 'wider' mapping as if it were 'equivalent' can silently lose meaning.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: NamingSystem is the resource that formally registers an identifier or code system's naming scheme — it links an OID, say, to its canonical FHIR URI, and records who owns it.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: TerminologyCapabilities is CapabilityStatement's cousin, but scoped to terminology services — it declares which code systems and value sets a given terminology server supports, plus what expansion parameters it honors.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So if you need to know whether a server can resolve a particular OID, or whether its $expand endpoint supports a given parameter, TerminologyCapabilities is where you'd look.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: They're easy to overlook, but they're exactly the kind of narrowly-scoped conformance resource the exam likes to test recognition of.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Required is the strictest binding strength — the coded element SHALL come from that exact value set, full stop, no substitutions.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That's why administrative codes like AdministrativeGender are usually required-bound — there's no legitimate reason to send a code outside that tiny set.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: If validation sees a code outside a required value set, that's a hard failure, not just a warning.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So required means the value set is exhaustive for that use — nothing else is conformant, which is the opposite end from example binding.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Extensible means you SHOULD use a code from the value set, but if none of the concepts actually fit the real-world situation, you're allowed to use a code from outside it.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: The catch is you can't just skip the value set when a suitable code does exist in it — extensible only excuses you when there's genuinely no fit.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: It's a common middle ground for clinical concepts like Condition.code, where the preferred value set is broad but can't realistically cover every diagnosis.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: On the exam, extensible is the one where 'no matching concept' is the justification for going outside it — otherwise you're expected to use the value set.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Preferred is a much looser binding — the value set is just a recommendation, and implementers are free to use codes from other systems entirely.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It shows up where there's no single dominant terminology for a concept, so FHIR suggests one but won't enforce it.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Validators generally won't flag a preferred-bound element for using an outside code — it's guidance, not a rule.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So on a spectrum from required down to example, preferred sits just above example — recommended, not mandated.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Example is the weakest binding — the value set is purely illustrative, just there to show the kind of codes you might use.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: There's no conformance expectation at all — using a totally different code system doesn't violate anything.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: You'll see it on elements where FHIR genuinely can't predict every use case across every implementation, so it just gives a sample instead of dictating one.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Recognize it by name on the exam — if a question says 'example binding,' any reasonable coding is acceptable, no exceptions needed.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: $expand takes a ValueSet's definition — its compose rules — and returns the actual, explicit list of codes it resolves to, which is what a picklist UI would use.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: $validate-code checks whether a specific code, or a whole Coding, is actually a valid member of a given ValueSet or CodeSystem.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: You'd run $expand to build a dropdown, then $validate-code later to confirm what a user picked, or what came in on a resource, is still conformant.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Both operations exist because bindings reference value sets abstractly — these are how you turn that abstraction into something concrete and checkable.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: $lookup takes a system and code and gives you back the details — display text, definition, and any properties the CodeSystem defines for it.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: $subsumes tests the hierarchy relationship between two codes — does one subsume the other, are they equivalent, or unrelated — which only makes sense for systems with real hierarchy, like SNOMED CT.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So $lookup answers 'what does this code mean,' while $subsumes answers 'how do these two codes relate to each other.'

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Subsumption testing is what lets a query for a broad SNOMED concept correctly match all its more specific descendants.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: $translate runs a ConceptMap to convert a code from one system to its equivalent in another — that's your terminology translation workhorse.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: $closure is more specialized — it maintains an incremental table of subsumption relationships over time, so a client can keep asking 'does this new code fit my existing table' without re-deriving the whole hierarchy each time.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: It's built for things like mobile or offline apps that need fast local subsumption checks without hitting a full terminology server repeatedly.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So translate moves a code across systems, and closure is about efficiently tracking hierarchy relationships incrementally — different jobs entirely.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: SNOMED CT is the clinical terminology — conditions, findings, procedures, body structures — and it's compositional, so you can combine concepts to express something precise.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: LOINC is built for observations and labs specifically — each code identifies what's measured, using axes like component, property, timing, system, and scale.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So a diagnosis of diabetes is SNOMED, but the hemoglobin A1c lab test that helped diagnose it is LOINC — they're not interchangeable.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Common exam trap: picking SNOMED for a lab test code or LOINC for a condition — match the terminology to what's actually being coded.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: ICD-10-CM is diagnosis coding for the US, and it's really administrative and billing-oriented rather than clinically granular.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: You'll see it on Condition.code in claims contexts, and definitely on Claim.diagnosis, since payers require it for reimbursement.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: It's coarser than SNOMED CT for clinical documentation, which is exactly why US Core often binds Condition to SNOMED preferentially while still accommodating ICD-10-CM for billing.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So if a scenario is about claims or reimbursement, think ICD-10-CM; if it's about clinical decision support, SNOMED is usually the better fit.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: CPT codes describe procedures and professional services — they're AMA-maintained and show up on Procedure.code and claim line items for what a clinician actually did.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: HCPCS Level II fills the gaps CPT doesn't cover — durable medical equipment, supplies, ambulance services, certain drugs — anything that isn't a physician procedure per se.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Both are fundamentally billing terminologies, so you'll see them heavily in Claim and ExplanationOfBenefit resources under CARIN Blue Button.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: If the scenario is 'what procedure was billed' versus 'what equipment or supply was billed,' that's your CPT versus HCPCS split.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: RxNorm normalizes medication names — ingredient, strength, and dose form — into one standard code, which is what MedicationRequest and MedicationStatement.code typically use.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: NDC, the National Drug Code, is more granular — it identifies a specific manufactured, packaged product, which matters for dispensing and billing where package size and manufacturer actually count.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: So RxNorm answers 'what medication is this, conceptually,' while NDC answers 'which exact package did the pharmacy dispense.'

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Prescribing usually rides on RxNorm; dispensing and claims usually need the NDC alongside it.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: UCUM is the coded system for units of measure — instead of a free-text 'mg/dL,' you get a machine-computable unit code that any conformant system parses the same way.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It shows up in Quantity.code alongside Quantity.unit, and it's what lets two systems safely compare or convert lab values instead of guessing from display text.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Without a UCUM code, a value of 'mg/dL' is just a string — nothing stops a receiving system from misreading the units entirely.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So anywhere you see Quantity in a clinical resource, expect UCUM doing the real semantic work behind the scenes.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Authentication answers who you are; authorization answers what you're allowed to do — FHIR handles both through SMART on FHIR, built on OAuth2 and OpenID Connect.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: For interactive apps like a patient portal, you use the authorization code flow. For backend services with no user present, it's client credentials instead.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Either way, scopes limit exactly what the token can touch, and launch context tells the app which patient or user it's operating for.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: And watch the token lifecycle — a 401 means your token's bad or expired, a 403 means you're authenticated but not allowed, so refresh or re-scope accordingly.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Confidentiality and integrity go beyond just locking down access — they're about who touched the data and why.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Consent directives control whether access is even permitted, Provenance records who created or changed a resource, and AuditEvent logs who accessed it.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Minimization matters too — only expose the data that's actually needed for the stated purpose of use.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Here's the trap: getting past OAuth doesn't mean you've satisfied consent. Authorization success and consent compliance are two separate checks.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Auditability is about proving, after the fact, who did what to a resource and when.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: In FHIR that's the AuditEvent resource — it captures the actor, the action like read or update, the entity affected, and the outcome.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Good audit design means every access to sensitive data — not just writes — gets logged, so you can reconstruct a full access history.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: On the exam, if a question asks which resource proves an access event happened, the answer's AuditEvent — Provenance is about authorship, not access logging.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Minimization means don't hand over more data than the requesting purpose actually needs.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Purpose of use narrows a request — a billing system doesn't need psych notes, and a consent policy or scope should reflect that limit.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: meta.security labels can carry that policy right on the resource, flagging sensitive categories like substance-abuse data.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Just remember, a valid access token doesn't override the minimization obligation — consent and purpose still shape what actually gets returned.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Two OAuth grant types matter most for FHIR: authorization code and client credentials.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Authorization code is for apps with a user present — a patient logging into a portal app that then talks to the FHIR server.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Client credentials skips the user entirely — it's for backend, system-to-system services authenticating as themselves, not on behalf of anyone.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Exam tip: if a patient opens an app to see their own chart, that's SMART plus authorization code — not a backend batch job.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: SMART on FHIR issues more than one kind of token. The access token is what you actually present to the FHIR server.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: The refresh token lets you get a new access token without making the user log in again, since access tokens are deliberately short-lived.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: If OpenID Connect is layered on top, you also get an id_token, which carries identity claims about the user, not resource access.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: So a 401 on an otherwise-working app usually just means the access token expired — time to use the refresh token, not to re-authenticate from scratch.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Scopes are how a SMART token says exactly what it can touch — like patient/Observation.rs for read-only access to one patient's observations.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: They combine a context — patient or user — a resource type, and permitted interactions, so the server can enforce fine-grained access.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: The token lifecycle then governs how long that access lasts: issue, use, expire, refresh, and eventually revoke.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: If a call suddenly fails with 401, check the lifecycle first — it's often just expiry, not a scope problem.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: SMART on FHIR defines two launch flows: EHR launch and standalone launch.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: EHR launch starts inside the EHR itself — the user clicks your app from within their workflow, and the EHR hands you an initial launch context.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Standalone launch is the opposite — the app starts on its own, outside any EHR session, and has to let the user pick the patient during authorization.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Same OAuth mechanics underneath, but which one applies changes how — and from whom — you get that first launch context.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Before an app can even request a token, it needs to discover the server's OAuth endpoints — that's what the .well-known/smart-configuration document is for.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: It advertises the authorization and token endpoints, supported scopes, and capabilities like whether dynamic client registration is available.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Then the app requests scopes matching what it actually needs — something narrow like patient/Condition.rs rather than a blanket grant.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Hardcoding endpoints instead of discovering them is a common implementer mistake — the whole point of SMART is that clients discover capabilities dynamically.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Launch context is how the app learns who it's acting for — which patient, and which authenticated user.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: That context arrives as extra parameters in the token response — a patient parameter with the Patient id, sometimes a separate user or encounter context too.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Without it, the app has a perfectly valid token but no idea whose chart to open.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: Exam tip: scopes and launch context work together — the scope says what's allowed, the context says for whom.

conversation.speaker: maya
conversation.text: Backend services in SMART on FHIR are for system-to-system integration — no user clicking through a login screen.

conversation.speaker: alex
conversation.text: The client authenticates with a signed JWT assertion instead of a shared secret, proving it holds a private key registered with the server.

conversation.speaker: maya
